passages.t: The kings of the north, and their chariots
passages.happening:
The scene moves north. Jabin, king of Hazor, hears what has happened in the south and gathers a great alliance. He sends to the kings of Madon, Shimron and Achshaph, to the kings of the northern hills and the valley south of the Sea of Chinnereth, and to peoples as far as the foot of Mount Hermon (verses 1-3).

They come out with all their armies, ‘a multitude as numerous as the sand on the seashore, along with a great number of horses and chariots’ (verse 4). They camp together at the waters of Merom.

The LORD speaks to Joshua. “Do not be afraid of them, for by this time tomorrow I will deliver all of them slain before Israel. You are to hamstring their horses and burn up their chariots” (verse 6).

Joshua and his army come on them suddenly and attack. The LORD gives them into Israel's hand, and Israel pursues them a long way north and east (verses 7-8). Joshua does as he was told with the horses and chariots (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Hazor stood north of the Sea of Galilee, which this chapter calls Chinnereth. It was the largest city in Canaan in that age, with a high inner city and a wide lower town. It is named in letters and records of the ancient world from long before Joshua. When its king called, others came.

This is the largest force Israel has faced, and it has something Israel does not have. Chariots were the most advanced weapon of the time. They were light, fast, two-wheeled carts drawn by trained horses, and the armies of Egypt and of the Canaanite cities used them. Israel was a people on foot.

God's command about the horses and chariots is the surprising part. An army that captures the best weapons of its day normally keeps them. Israel is told to destroy them. To hamstring a horse was to cut the tendon of its hind leg so that it could never again be used in war. The chariots were to be burned.

The point was that Israel must not come to trust in such things. The law of Moses said that Israel's future king must not build up a great force of horses. The Psalms and the prophets say again and again that horses and chariots cannot save. Israel was to win this battle and walk away from it no better armed than before, so that the next time it would still have to depend on God.

The battle itself is told in two verses. As at Gibeon, Joshua moves fast and strikes without warning. The writer gives the credit in the usual place: ‘the LORD delivered them into the hand of Israel’.

The laming of the horses is hard for a modern reader who cares about animals. It belongs to the warfare of its time, and the text gives it as an order about weapons. It is not offered as a way to treat any creature now.
passages.later:
The law for Israel's king reads, “But the king must not acquire many horses for himself” (Deuteronomy 17:16).

A psalm draws the lesson: “No king is saved by his vast army; no warrior is delivered by his great strength. A horse is a vain hope for salvation; even its great strength cannot save” (Psalm 33:16-17).
passages.asks: Israel was told to burn the chariots it had just won. Ask what advantage has come into your hands that you are beginning to lean on more than you lean on God: money, standing, skill, a powerful friend. Ask what it would look like to hold it loosely. And ask what you are counting when you feel outnumbered.

passages.t: Hazor burned, and the cities left standing
passages.happening:
Joshua turns back and takes Hazor, ‘because Hazor was formerly the head of all these kingdoms’ (verse 10). Its king is killed. The people of the city are put to the sword and devoted to destruction, and the city is burned (verse 11).

The other royal cities of the north are taken and their kings killed, ‘as Moses the LORD’s servant had commanded’ (verse 12).

Then the writer adds a detail. “Yet Israel did not burn any of the cities built on their mounds, except Hazor, which Joshua burned” (verse 13). Israel takes the goods and livestock of these cities. The people are put to the sword (verse 14).

The passage closes with a chain of command. “As the LORD had commanded His servant Moses, so Moses commanded Joshua. That is what Joshua did, leaving nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses” (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Verses 11 and 14 say that no one who breathed was left. The words are the words of the command in Deuteronomy, and they carry the same weight as at Jericho. The note on chapter 6, verses 17 to 21, sets out the ways Christians read them, the cost of each, and what holds on every reading. Nothing in this chapter gives anyone a warrant for violence against any person or people.

Verse 13 is one of the most important sentences in the book for understanding what the conquest was. Ancient towns were built again and again on the ruins of older ones, so that over centuries they rose on low hills of their own making. Those are the ‘mounds’. Israel burned only one of them. The rest were left standing, because Israel was going to live in them. Moses had said that Israel would receive cities it did not build and houses it did not fill.

So Joshua's own account names three burned cities in all: Jericho, Ai and Hazor. A reader who pictures the whole land in flames has pictured more than the book says.

Hazor has been dug by archaeologists. They found that the great city was destroyed by a fierce fire, usually dated to the thirteenth century BC. Some of those who dug it connected the fire with Israel. Others have proposed the Egyptians, a rival Canaanite city, or a revolt from within. Scholars who place Joshua earlier look to an earlier layer of the ruins. The book page sets this out and takes no side.

The last verse is about Joshua. The book has measured him from the start by one standard, whether he did what Moses was told. It says that he left nothing undone. That is a statement about his obedience, and the writer means it as praise. It does not settle the questions a reader brings to verses 11 and 14.
passages.later:
Moses had described the gift in advance: ‘a land with great and splendid cities that you did not build’ (Deuteronomy 6:10).

God says the same at the end of this book, looking back: “So I gave you a land on which you did not toil and cities that you did not build, and now you live in them and eat from vineyards and olive groves that you did not plant” (Joshua 24:13).
passages.asks: Israel moved into towns it had not built and ate from vines it had not planted. Ask what you live in, use and enjoy every day that someone else made: a house, a language, a church, a faith handed down. Ask whether you treat it as earned. Then bring to God what troubles you in verses 11 and 14, and do not let anyone tell you that being troubled is unbelief.

passages.t: A long war, hardened hearts, and rest
passages.happening:
The writer sums up. Joshua took the hill country, the Negev, the foothills, the Jordan valley and the mountains, from the far south to the foot of Mount Hermon in the north (verses 16-17).

It did not happen quickly. “Joshua waged war against all these kings for a long period of time” (verse 18).

“No city made peace with the Israelites except the Hivites living in Gibeon; all others were taken in battle” (verse 19). The writer gives a reason that stops the reader: ‘For it was of the LORD to harden their hearts to engage Israel in battle’ (verse 20).

Joshua also defeats the Anakim, the people of great height in the southern hills. None are left in Israel's land. Some remain in Gaza, Gath and Ashdod (verses 21-22).

“So Joshua took the entire land, in keeping with all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it as an inheritance to Israel according to the allotments to their tribes. Then the land had rest from war” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 10 and 11 can be read in a few minutes, and they sound like a few weeks of fighting. Verse 18 corrects that. The war was long. Caleb's ages, given in chapter 14, suggest about seven years.

Verse 19 looks back at Gibeon. Every other city fought. The verse shows that peace had been possible. One group of Canaanites asked for it and received it. Rahab had found mercy in the same way.

The Anakim were the people who had terrified the scouts forty years before. The scouts said they felt like grasshoppers beside them, and that fear kept a whole generation out of the land. Now the same people are overcome. The writer notes that a few remained in three towns on the coast. One of those towns is Gath, and a reader who knows the story of David will remember where Goliath came from.

The last verse says Joshua took ‘the entire land’. Chapter 13 will open with God saying that very much of the land is still untaken. The book places these statements two chapters apart. Many readers take the first to speak of the land as a whole, with its kings broken and no power left that could stand against Israel, and the second of all that had yet to be settled. Others hear in the first the sweeping style of ancient victory reports. Either way, a reader needs both statements to hear what the book is saying.

‘Rest’ is the word chapter 1 promised. Here it means that the fighting stopped.
passages.later:
The scouts had said of the Anakim, ‘We seemed like grasshoppers in our own sight’ (Numbers 13:33). Moses told the next generation what to remember when they heard people say, “Who can stand up to the sons of Anak?” (Deuteronomy 9:2).

The letter to the Hebrews looks back on this rest and says it was not the last: “For if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day. There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:8-9).
passages.hard:
What does it mean that the LORD hardened the hearts of the Canaanite kings?

The words recall the story of Pharaoh in Exodus, whose heart is said to be hardened by God and also by himself. “But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exodus 9:12). ‘He hardened his heart and would not listen’ (Exodus 8:15).

Christians have understood such verses in two main ways.

Some stress God's rule over all things, the human heart included. On this view God brought about the kings' resolve to fight as part of his judgment.

Others stress that God confirmed a stubbornness that was already there. The kings had heard what the LORD had done. Rahab and the Gibeonites heard the same reports and sought peace. The kings chose war, and God gave them over to the path they had chosen.

These notes do not choose between the two. On either view the text holds the kings responsible for what they did, and it shows that the way of peace had been open, since Gibeon took it. The doctrine study on God's rule and human choice says more.

The verse must not be used to say of any person or people today that God has hardened them. No reader is given that knowledge about anyone.
passages.asks: The war took years, though it reads like days. Ask what long obedience you are in the middle of, and whether you had expected it to be quick. Then think about the Anakim, the old fear that had kept a generation out. Ask what fear you inherited from those who went before you, and whether it is as large as you were told.
